title: Stagira to Chalcis: the Master of Those Who Know
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Stagira and the Garden of the Academy

stops.name: Stagira, the house of Nicomachus the physician
stops.campa: In the small Chalcidic city of Stagira, on the northern Aegean, a son is born to Nicomachus, physician and friend to Amyntas III, king of Macedon, and to Phaestis, a woman of Chalcidian stock. The father's craft traces itself, the family says, to Asclepius the healer, seven generations back. The boy is named Aristotle. Because of the father's office at court, the child spends part of his boyhood at Pella among the sons of the Macedonian nobility, learning early the ways of kings that he will one day be paid to teach to a king's own son.
suggested_refs: The archaeological site of ancient Stagira, above the bay of Olympiada, Halkidiki
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.1

stops.name: Pella, among the sons of the Macedonian court
stops.campa: At Pella, the low new capital Archelaus built for the kings of Macedon, the physician's son is raised for a time among courtiers and companions of the royal house. He watches his father dose and dress the wounds of Amyntas and learns, before he ever opens a book of philosophy, the smell of a palace and the temper of a king. The connection sown here, between the house of Nicomachus and the house of the Argeads, will not be broken; it will be called upon again in another generation, for another king's son.
suggested_refs: The archaeological site of ancient Pella, capital of Macedon
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.1

stops.name: Stagira, orphaned, the ward of Proxenus
stops.campa: Both parents die while Aristotle is still a boy. Guardianship falls to Proxenus of Atarneus, a family friend, who raises him with his own son Nicanor as a brother and sees that he wants for nothing in his schooling. It is a debt Aristotle will not forget: decades later his will still provides for Nicanor's children as for his own blood, and asks that statues of Zeus and Athena the Saviours be raised at Stagira in thanks for a safe return, in memory of the guardian who stood in a father's place.
suggested_refs: The clause of Aristotle's will providing for Nicanor and the house of Proxenus
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.11-16 (the will)

stops.name: Athens, the Academy in the grove of Akademos
stops.campa: At seventeen Aristotle comes down to Athens and enters the Academy of Plato, in the olive grove named for the hero Akademos outside the walls. He will stay nearly twenty years, the most durable pupil that school ever has. He buys books at a rate the other young men think eccentric, reads late by lamplight, and argues with a thoroughness that unsettles his elders. He is, by every later account, Plato's most genuine disciple, though the two men's minds will pull, over the years, toward very different ends.
suggested_refs: The archaeological park of Akadimia Platonos, Athens, site of Plato's Academy
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.1
Wikisource, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book V

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, called 'the mind of the school'
stops.campa: The school comes to call his lodging house 'the house of the Reader', for a student who is forever at his rolls of papyrus rather than at play; and when Aristotle is absent from the lecture hall, Plato is said to remark that the audience has lost its mind, meaning Aristotle himself, whom he named nous, the intellect of the Academy. He is asked once what liars gain by lying, and answers only that when they do happen to speak the truth, they are not believed for it.
stops.quote: Just this, that when they speak the truth they are not believed.
stops.quote_source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V (sayings of Aristotle)
suggested_refs: The epithet 'nous of the school', preserved in the ancient Lives of Aristotle
sources: Wikisource, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book V

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the death of Plato
stops.campa: In his eighty-first year Plato dies, and the Academy passes not to Aristotle but to Speusippus, the founder's nephew, a mathematician of narrower cast. Aristotle does not contest it, but he does not stay to serve under it either. He gathers Xenocrates, a fellow member of the school, and prepares to leave the grove of Akademos for the courts of Asia Minor. Plato, in the years before, is said to have watched his brilliant pupil pull away and remarked that Aristotle spurned him, as a colt kicks out at the mother who bore it.
stops.quote: Aristotle spurns me, as colts kick out at the mother who bore them.
stops.quote_source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.2 (attributed to Plato)
suggested_refs: The site of Plato's tomb within the grove of the Academy, Athens
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.1-2

segments.name: Assos and the Court of Hermias

stops.name: Assos, at the court of Hermias of Atarneus
stops.campa: Aristotle and Xenocrates cross to the Troad and the cliff-town of Assos, ruled by Hermias, a former slave and eunuch who bought his way to a small tyranny and had once, like them, sat in the Academy. Hermias throws the fortress open to philosophers; on the rock above the strait toward Lesbos a second Academy takes shape in miniature, arguing physics and politics within sight of the sea. Aristotle, cut loose from Athens, finds in this rough Aeolian court the freedom to found a school of his own devising.
suggested_refs: The acropolis and temple of Athena at Assos, above the court of Hermias
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.3

stops.name: Assos, the school among the rocks, Callisthenes and Theophrastus
stops.campa: Around Hermias's citadel a circle gathers: Xenocrates, the young Theophrastus, come over already from nearby Lesbos, and Aristotle's own grand-nephew Callisthenes of Olynthus, a boy he will, in time, present to a prince and thereby doom. They work on logic, on politics, on the classification of living things, testing a method of inquiry that owes debts to Plato and quarrels with him in equal measure. It is here, more than in the Academy's grove, that the shape of Aristotle's own philosophy first hardens into something distinct.
suggested_refs: The Troad coast between Assos and Lesbos, crossed constantly by the circle of scholars

stops.name: Assos, marriage to Pythias
stops.campa: Aristotle marries Pythias, called in different accounts the niece and the adopted daughter of Hermias, a young woman raised in the tyrant's own household. She bears him, within the marriage's short span, a daughter she names for herself. It is by every report a close and grieving marriage: when Pythias dies some years later, Aristotle's own will still asks that her bones be laid, wherever his own come to rest, exactly as she herself instructed before her death.
suggested_refs: The clause of Aristotle's will directing that Pythias's bones be reunited with his own
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.11-16 (the will)

stops.name: Mytilene, removal to Lesbos with Theophrastus
stops.campa: At the urging of Theophrastus, a native of Eresos on the island, Aristotle crosses with Pythias to Lesbos and settles near Mytilene. Together they open a second circle on the model of the Academy, but bent now toward the natural world rather than pure dialectic. Fishermen and farmers of the island bring them specimens, shells, and reports of strange creatures of the deep water; between the two men a division of labor begins that will define natural history for two thousand years, Theophrastus turning to the plants, Aristotle to the animals.
suggested_refs: The city of Mytilene, Lesbos, seat of the joint school of Aristotle and Theophrastus

stops.name: The lagoon of Pyrrha, the dissections begin
stops.campa: The landlocked lagoon at Pyrrha, in the island's center, becomes Aristotle's favored laboratory: a shallow, warm, and teeming water where the whole variety of marine life can be taken close to shore and studied at leisure. He dissects and classifies with an exactness no one before him has attempted, describing the reproduction of the dogfish, the habits of the octopus, the anatomy of the cuttlefish, laying the ground of the History of Animals and the Parts of Animals. Two millennia later a naturalist bound for the Beagle will still praise the precision of what is done here.
suggested_refs: The Gulf of Kalloni (ancient Pyrrha), Lesbos, still a naturalist's site

stops.name: Mytilene, a daughter born, called Pythias
stops.campa: Amid the lagoon work and the school's daily arguments, Pythias bears a daughter, given her own mother's name. The household on Lesbos is, by the accounts that survive of Aristotle's private habits, an orderly and affectionate one: he is said to keep a fixed hour for bathing, to be particular about his dress and his rings, and to speak with something of a lisp, a small human detail the ancient biographers thought worth recording of a man mostly remembered for the size of his mind.
suggested_refs: The line of Aristotle's descendants through his daughter Pythias, later married to Nicanor
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.1, 11-16

stops.name: Mytilene, the summons from Pella
stops.campa: A letter comes from Philip II, king of Macedon, the man whose father's court Aristotle knew as a boy: his son Alexander, thirteen years old and already impatient of ordinary tutors, is to be given the finest teacher Greece can furnish. Whatever the two years at Pyrrha have still to yield, Aristotle sets it aside. He and Theophrastus part, their fields of the world already half-divided between beast and plant, and Aristotle sails north and west for Macedon, back toward the court his father served.
suggested_refs: Philip II's letter of invitation, referenced in the ancient Lives of Aristotle
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.4

segments.name: Pella and Mieza: Tutor of the King's Son

stops.name: Pella, presented to Philip and to Alexander
stops.campa: Aristotle returns to the low palace of Pella where he once ran as a physician's son among other men's sons, and is presented now to the boy he is to teach: Alexander, restless, quick, already half in love with Achilles and the Iliad. Philip receives the philosopher as an equal, not a hireling; the terms of the arrangement, the canon insists, will bind the king as much as the tutor, for Aristotle asks a price no gold could set: the rebuilding of his own ruined city.
suggested_refs: The palace of Pella, where the arrangement for Alexander's education was struck
sources: GreekReporter.com, 'Mieza: The School Where Aristotle Tutored Alexander the Great'

stops.name: Stagira, the ruined city rebuilt at the tutor's word
stops.campa: Six years before, Philip's campaigns had leveled Stagira and scattered or enslaved its people, punishment for standing against Macedon with the Chalcidic League. Now, as the price of taking Alexander in hand, Aristotle asks the city restored and its exiles brought home; Philip agrees and rebuilds it from the ground. The men of Stagira will remember the debt after his death: they raise an altar over his tomb, name him founder of the refounded city, and keep an annual festival in his honor, the Aristoteleia.
suggested_refs: The rebuilt ruins of Stagira and the later Aristoteleia festival kept in his memory

stops.name: Mieza, the Nymphaeum, the school of caves and terraces
stops.campa: For quiet and for shade Philip sets the school not in the palace but at Mieza, in the country south of Pella, at a sanctuary of the Nymphs cut into limestone terraces above a stream, with natural caves at its heart. Here Aristotle gathers Alexander and the young men who will become his companions and marshals, Hephaestion, Ptolemy, and others of high Macedonian blood, and teaches them ethics, politics, natural science, medicine, and the poets, walking the porticoed terraces as he later will the peripatos of the Lyceum.
suggested_refs: The Nymphaeum of Mieza, near modern Naousa, its caves and terraces still visible
sources: GreekReporter.com, 'New Archaeological Evidence... Aristotle's School in Mieza'

stops.name: Mieza, word of Hermias's betrayal and death
stops.campa: Word reaches the school at Mieza that Hermias has been taken. The Persian commander Mentor of Rhodes lured him to a parley under false truce, seized him, and sent him in chains to the Great King, where under torture he was asked to betray Macedon's designs on Asia; he is said to have answered nothing worth the name of treachery, and died, some say by crucifixion, still loyal to the friend and pupil he had sheltered at Assos. Aristotle, who owed him a wife, a school, and years of safety, receives the news like the death of kin.
suggested_refs: The death of Hermias of Atarneus, recorded across the ancient biographical tradition
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.3

stops.name: Mieza, the Hymn to Virtue composed for the fallen friend
stops.campa: In Hermias's memory Aristotle composes a skolion, a hymn to Virtue in the shape of a paean, and has it sung; it will outlive him by centuries, preserved whole by later writers, and it is this hymn, sung for a mortal man in the manner owed to a god, that a hostile Athens will one day use against him. For now it is only grief set to verse, the philosopher's promise that no gold, no parents, no soft-eyed sleep is dearer than the courage his friend showed at the end.
stops.quote: Such courage dost thou implant in the mind, imperishable, better than gold, dearer than parents or soft-eyed sleep.
stops.quote_source: The Hymn to Virtue (Hymn to Hermias), preserved in Diogenes Laertius, Book V, and Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae XV
suggested_refs: The Hymn to Virtue, Aristotle's skolion for Hermias, the ancient world's most famous philosophical poem
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V
R. Renehan, 'Aristotle as Lyric Poet: The Hermias Poem'

stops.name: Mieza, the annotated Iliad, a king's viaticum
stops.campa: Among the texts Aristotle sets before his pupil, none matters more than Homer. He prepares for Alexander his own recension of the Iliad, corrected and annotated in his own hand, which the prince will keep under his pillow beside a dagger for the rest of his life, calling it his viaticum of the art of war. Years later, after Issus, Alexander will have it moved into a jeweled casket taken from the tent of Darius, judging nothing in the Persian king's baggage worthier of holding the book his teacher gave him.
suggested_refs: The 'casket copy' of the Iliad, Alexander's annotated text from Aristotle, carried on campaign

stops.name: Pella, Philip's death, the tutoring ends
stops.campa: Philip is assassinated at Aegae by his own bodyguard, and Alexander, not yet twenty, is proclaimed king in his place. The years of formal instruction had already loosened once Alexander began to stand in as regent for his campaigning father, and now they end outright: a king has no tutor, only counselors he may or may not still hear. Aristotle, his charge crowned, has no further office at the Macedonian court, and turns his eyes back to Athens, where a school of his own founding is still only an idea.
suggested_refs: Aegae (Vergina), site of Philip II's assassination and tomb

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum founded in the grove of Apollo
stops.campa: Aristotle returns to Athens, now under Alexander's shadow, and opens his own school in a public gymnasium sacred to Apollo Lyceius, east of the city walls. As a resident alien he cannot own the ground as Plato's heirs owned the Academy's grove, so the Lyceum stays half-public: many of its lectures, unlike the Academy's, are open and free. He walks the colonnaded peripatos while he teaches, a habit that gives his followers their lasting name, the Peripatetics, the walking philosophers.
suggested_refs: The archaeological site of the Lyceum, Rigillis Street, Athens

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, morning and afternoon lectures
stops.campa: The school settles a rhythm still copied by universities: in the morning, walking with his inner circle, Aristotle gives the hard esoteric lectures, logic, metaphysics, the close natural sciences, meant only for those already trained to follow; in the afternoon, before a wider public, the exoteric lectures on rhetoric and politics, open to any Athenian who cares to listen. When Alexander later complains by letter that the deeper lectures have been written down and might now be read by anyone, Aristotle answers that they are published and not published, since they will mean nothing to those who never heard them argued.
stops.quote: The doctrines of which he spoke were both published and not published; for in truth his treatise on metaphysics is of no use for those who would either teach or learn the science, but is written as a memorandum for those already trained therein.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander, chapter 7 (Perrin translation)
suggested_refs: The distinction of esoteric and exoteric works, recorded by Plutarch and Aulus Gellius

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, the great collection assembled
stops.campa: As Alexander's armies push east, Pliny will later record that the king ordered hunters, fowlers, and fishermen the length of Asia and Greece to send back to Aristotle every strange beast, egg, or shell they found, an outlay put at eight hundred talents. Whatever the true sum, the Lyceum fills with specimens, maps, and manuscripts beyond any library Athens has seen, the working stock for the History of Animals and the treatises still to come. Theophrastus works at his side on the plants; between them the two great catalogues of nature take their first systematic shape.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Elder's account (Natural History VIII.44) of Alexander's specimens sent to Aristotle
sources: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book VIII.44

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, Pythias dies, Herpyllis and Nicomachus
stops.campa: Some ten years into the marriage Pythias dies, and Aristotle, past fifty now, takes as companion Herpyllis, a woman of his own Stagira, who bears him a son he names Nicomachus for his father. It is for this boy that the great treatise on the ethical life will one day be titled, the Nicomachean Ethics, whether compiled by the father for the son or by the son from the father's lectures the ancient sources do not agree. Asked once what a friend is, Aristotle gives the answer that outlives every treatise: a single soul dwelling in two bodies.
stops.quote: A single soul dwelling in two bodies.
stops.quote_source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V (sayings of Aristotle, on friendship)
suggested_refs: The Nicomachean Ethics, named for Aristotle's son Nicomachus
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, news of Callisthenes's death in Asia
stops.campa: Callisthenes, Aristotle's grand-nephew, sent east years before on his teacher's own recommendation to write the history of the campaign, refuses at the Bactrian court to perform the Persian obeisance Alexander now demands, and is caught up soon after in the Pages' Conspiracy and put to death, whether by hanging, prison-fever, or the rack the accounts do not agree. The news reaches the Lyceum like a small crack across a great friendship: Alexander's letters to his old tutor grow colder, though the specimens, oddly, keep arriving from Asia all the same.
suggested_refs: Callisthenes of Olynthus, historian of Alexander's campaign, executed in the Pages' Conspiracy

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, the great treatises taking shape
stops.campa: Through these Athenian years the bulk of what will survive as Aristotle's corpus is drafted and redrafted as lecture notes for the school: the Physics, the Metaphysics (a name no one yet uses, since the word does not exist), the Politics, the Poetics, the Rhetoric, On the Soul. None are polished for a reading public; they are closer to a teacher's dense working papers than to books, which is precisely why, when they are lost and refound centuries later, the world will find in them a mind still thinking rather than a mind already finished.
suggested_refs: The corpus of Aristotle's Lyceum treatises: Physics, Metaphysics, Politics, Poetics, Rhetoric, On the Soul

stops.name: Athens, the Lyceum, on truth dearer than a friend
stops.campa: Late in the Lyceum years, weighing the doctrine of Forms he was taught in Plato's own grove and has since come to doubt, Aristotle sets down the sentence that will be quoted longer than almost anything else he writes: that though both truth and his old friends are dear to him, piety requires him to honor truth above his friends. It is the clearest signal the canon preserves of how far the pupil has traveled from the master who once called him, half in reproach, a colt that kicked at its own mother.
stops.quote: While both are dear, piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.
stops.quote_source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, chapter 6, 1096a16 (Ross translation)
suggested_refs: 'Amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas,' the Latin tag drawn from this passage of the Ethics
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V

stops.name: Athens, news of Alexander's death in Babylon
stops.campa: Word comes to the Lyceum that Alexander has died of fever in Babylon, not yet thirty-three, the empire he built already splitting among his generals before his body is embalmed. In Athens the news breaks like a dam: the city that has chafed under Macedonian garrisons for a decade rises in what will be called the Lamian War, and every man remembered as a friend of Macedon, however old, however retired from politics, becomes a mark for the city's anger. Aristotle, tutor of the dead conqueror, is exactly such a man.
suggested_refs: The Lamian War (323-322 BC), Athens's uprising after Alexander's death
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V

stops.name: Athens, the charge of impiety over the Hymn to Hermias
stops.campa: Eurymedon the hierophant of the Eleusinian mysteries, with one Demophilus, lays a formal charge of impiety against Aristotle: the old hymn sung thirty years before for the murdered Hermias, they say, honored a mortal man with the words owed only to a god. It is the same law, the same accusation of asebeia, that killed Socrates seventy-six years before in this same city. Aristotle, unlike Socrates, does not choose to stand trial and drink what the court decrees.
suggested_refs: Eurymedon the Hierophant and the charge of impiety against Aristotle, 323 BC
sources: GreekReporter.com, 'Why Did Aristotle Flee Athens When Indicted Rather Than Die Like Socrates?'

stops.name: Athens, departure, 'lest Athens sin twice against philosophy'
stops.campa: Rather than answer the charge, Aristotle leaves the Lyceum to Theophrastus and withdraws to his mother's family estate at Chalcis, across the strait in Euboea, out of Athenian jurisdiction. He gives, and the whole later tradition repeats, the reason for going rather than staying to argue as Socrates once argued: he will not give the Athenians occasion to sin twice against philosophy. It is the single sentence for which, after all the treatises, many will remember him longest.
stops.quote: I will not allow the Athenians to sin twice against philosophy.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Aristotle at his departure from Athens, preserved in the later biographical tradition (Aelian, Varia Historia; cf. Diogenes Laertius, Book V)
suggested_refs: The strait of the Euripus between Athens's territory and Chalcis, crossed in the flight
sources: GreekReporter.com, 'Why Did Aristotle Flee Athens When Indicted Rather Than Die Like Socrates?'

stops.name: Chalcis, the mother's estate, a fragment on solitude
stops.campa: At Chalcis, cut off from the school he built and the city that tried him, Aristotle keeps writing. A line from one of his private letters survives only because a later rhetorician quotes it as a model of style, and it says more of these last months than any treatise: the more solitary and alone he has become, he writes, the more he has come to love the old myths and their stories, as if logic itself needed, at the end, the company of wonder.
stops.quote: The more solitary and alone I am, the fonder I have become of myths.
stops.quote_source: Aristotle, fragment of a letter, preserved in Demetrius, On Style, section 144
suggested_refs: The fragments of Aristotle's private letters, preserved only in later rhetorical quotation

stops.name: Chalcis, the will is dictated
stops.campa: Aristotle dictates his testament, preserved whole by Diogenes Laertius three centuries on. Antipater, Alexander's regent in Macedon, is named executor over all; Nicanor, ward of the house of Proxenus, is to marry the daughter Pythias and stand as father and brother to the boy Nicomachus; Herpyllis, who has been good to him, is to be given a talent of silver, three handmaids, and her choice of houses, and married again if she wishes it, to a man not unworthy. Several slaves are freed outright; others are freed on conditions of continued service. Every clause reads like a man closing accounts with unusual tenderness.
stops.quote: The executors and Nicanor, in memory of me and of the steady affection which Herpyllis has borne towards me, shall take care of her in every other respect and, if she desires to be married, shall see that she be given to one not unworthy.
stops.quote_source: Aristotle's will, preserved in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.11-16
suggested_refs: The complete text of Aristotle's will, uniquely preserved by Diogenes Laertius
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book V.11-16

stops.name: Chalcis, death by the Euripus
stops.campa: Aristotle dies at Chalcis in his sixty-third year, of a wasting stomach ailment his own household recognizes and records. It is only centuries later, among Christian writers eager to picture the greatest of the pagan philosophers broken at last by a mystery he could not master, that a different death is told: that he flung himself into the Euripus below the town, maddened by the strait's four daily reversals of current, crying out that since Aristotle could not comprehend the Euripus, let the Euripus take Aristotle instead. The tides of the strait, in fact, would not be explained by any science until the twentieth century.
stops.quote: Since Aristotle did not grasp the Euripus, let the Euripus grasp Aristotle.
stops.quote_source: The legendary last words attributed to Aristotle by later Christian polemicists (Procopius of Gaza and others), reported in the modern scholarly tradition as apocryphal
suggested_refs: The Euripus Strait at Chalcis, whose tidal reversals gave rise to the death-legend
sources: Taylor & Francis, 'The Myth of Aristotle's Suicide'

segments.name: The Long Afterlife: the Book Finds Its Readers

stops.name: Rome, the buried library surfaces and is carried west
stops.campa: Theophrastus, dying, leaves the Lyceum's library to Neleus of Scepsis, whose heirs, fearing the book-hungry kings of Pergamon, hide Aristotle's own working papers in an underground cellar, where damp and worms gnaw them for a century and more. A bibliophile named Apellicon buys the ruin and botches its restoration; then Sulla, sacking Athens in 86 BC, carries the whole spoiled library off to Rome. There the grammarian Tyrannio and, after him, Andronicus of Rhodes edit and publish it properly at last, arranging one untitled set of essays 'after the Physics,' ta meta ta physika, and so giving the world, by an accident of shelving, the name Metaphysics.
suggested_refs: Andronicus of Rhodes's first-century BC edition of the Corpus Aristotelicum, the ancestor of every modern text
sources: ontology.co, 'The Rediscovery of the Corpus Aristotelicum'

stops.name: Baghdad, the House of Wisdom translates the Philosopher
stops.campa: In Baghdad, under Caliph al-Ma'mun, the Bayt al-Hikma gathers scholars to render the Greek inheritance into Arabic: Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his school, al-Kindi among the first patrons, turn the Rhetoric, the Poetics, the Metaphysics, the Categories, On the Soul, and more out of Syriac and Greek into the language of the new empire's learning. Aristotle becomes, in the vocabulary the Arabic tradition will fix on him, al-mu'allim al-awwal, the First Teacher, the philosopher, unqualified, needing no other name.
suggested_refs: The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) of Baghdad, engine of the Greek-Arabic translation movement

stops.name: Córdoba, Ibn Rushd, called the Commentator
stops.campa: In Almohad Córdoba, Abu'l-Walid Muhammad ibn Rushd, physician and qadi, writes the great commentaries, line by line through the Physics, the Metaphysics, On the Soul, stripping away centuries of Neoplatonic accretion to recover, as he believes, the philosopher's own argument beneath it. The Latin West, receiving him a century later, will simply call him the Commentator, as it calls Aristotle himself the Philosopher, so completely does one name imply the other by then.
suggested_refs: Averroes (Ibn Rushd) of Córdoba, 'the Great Commentator' on Aristotle

stops.name: Fustat, Maimonides reconciles the Philosopher with the Torah
stops.campa: In Fustat, old Cairo, the physician Moses ben Maimon, Córdoba-born and long since fled the Almohad persecutions, completes the Guide for the Perplexed in Judeo-Arabic: an attempt, using the very logic the Baghdad translators carried west, to hold Aristotelian rationalism and the law of Moses in the same hand without breaking either. The book will travel, translated into Hebrew and then Latin, into the arguments of Aquinas and the whole Scholastic century, one more channel by which the Stagirite returns, transfigured, into Europe.
suggested_refs: Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed (Dalalat al-Ha'irin), Fustat, 1190

stops.name: Toledo, the school of translators renders the Commentator into Latin
stops.campa: In reconquered Toledo, where Arabic, Hebrew, and Latin scholars work side by side, Michael Scot and others turn Ibn Rushd's commentaries, and through them Aristotle's own texts, into Latin for the first time in full. The universities of Paris and Oxford, which had banned the teaching of Aristotle's natural philosophy in 1210 for fear of the pantheism they read in it, spend the thirteenth century instead absorbing it whole, commentary and all, until the Philosopher becomes, in Aquinas's own phrase, simply that: the Philosopher.
suggested_refs: The Toledo School of Translators and the Latin Aristotle of the thirteenth century

stops.name: Oxford, Roger Bacon reads the Philosopher through the Arabic mirror
stops.campa: At Oxford and in Paris, the Franciscan Roger Bacon, steeped in Aristotle's natural philosophy through the Arabic commentaries and their often corrupted Latin renderings, presses Pope Clement IV in his Opus Maius for better texts, translated straight from the Greek, and for the experimental testing Aristotle himself had practiced at Pyrrha but which the schools had let harden into mere quotation. Bacon's own scientia experimentalis, mathematics wedded to observation, is a direct descendant of the biologist who once waded the Lesbos lagoon.
suggested_refs: Roger Bacon's Opus Maius (1267), addressed to Pope Clement IV

stops.name: The poem of Hell, the master of those who know
stops.campa: In his last exile, sheltered at Ravenna by Guido Novello da Polenta while the Comedy moves toward its end, Dante Alighieri places Aristotle in the Limbo of the virtuous pagans, in the noble castle of the philosophic family, seated above Socrates and Plato, above Democritus and Zeno, honored by all and looking on all: il maestro di color che sanno, the master of those who know. It is the highest a Christian poet of that age can raise a man born seven centuries before Christ, and it is not a small thing that he raises Aristotle highest of all.
stops.quote: vidi 'l maestro di color che sanno / seder tra filosofica famiglia
stops.quote_source: Dante Alighieri, Inferno, Canto IV, lines 131-132
suggested_refs: Dante's Inferno, Canto IV, the Limbo of the virtuous pagans, and its portrait of Aristotle
